incidents.question: Our nightly data-export Job keeps failing, and every morning kubectl get pods -l job-name=export lists about a dozen pods in Error state, each with 0 restarts, cluttering the namespace. A colleague's similar Job instead shows a single pod in CrashLoopBackOff with a growing restart count. Why do the two Jobs behave so differently, and which setting should we use?
incidents.reference_answer: The difference comes from the restartPolicy of the Pod template of each Job. With restartPolicy: Never, the kubelet does not restart the failed container: it declares the Pod failed, and the Job object then creates a replacement Pod. Every failure therefore leaves a new Pod in Error with 0 restarts, which creates a lot of 'junk' in the cluster. With restartPolicy: OnFailure, the failed Pod is rerun in place by the kubelet: the same Pod shows a growing restart count and ends in CrashLoopBackOff, because Kubernetes waits a bit before restarting it to avoid a crash loop eating node resources. Kubernetes: Up and Running recommends restartPolicy: OnFailure so failed Pods are rerun in place. In both cases the real problem is the program exiting with a non-zero code: read the error in the logs of the failed (or previous) container, fix it, and delete the Job to clean up the failed Pods.

explains that restartPolicy: OnFailure reruns the same Pod in place, hence a growing restart count and CrashLoopBackOff
recommends restartPolicy: OnFailure (or at least explains the trade-off)
states that the underlying cause is the program failing with a non-zero exit code and that the logs must be read

incidents.question: Each time we roll out a new version of our Java API, users get connection errors for about a minute even though the new pods show Running almost immediately. The application needs roughly 40 seconds to load its caches before it can answer requests, and the pod spec only defines a liveness probe. What explains the errors and how do we fix it?
incidents.reference_answer: Kubernetes distinguishes liveness from readiness. Liveness determines whether an application is running properly, and containers that fail liveness checks are restarted; it says nothing about whether the container can already serve traffic. Readiness describes when a container is ready to serve user requests: containers that fail readiness checks are removed from service load balancers, and the Service object tracks which Pods are ready through the readiness check. Applications often need some initialization time (from under a second to several minutes) before they can handle requests. Since the pods have no readiness check, nothing keeps the new pods out of the Service while their caches load, so requests reach pods that cannot answer yet. Fix: add a readiness probe (configured like a liveness probe) that only succeeds once the caches are loaded, and keep the liveness probe for detecting broken processes. When a readiness check fails, the endpoints of the Service change and kube-proxy rewrites its iptables rules so traffic only goes to ready pods.

explains that without a readiness check the new pods receive traffic while still initializing
recommends adding a readiness probe that succeeds only after initialization
mentions that pods failing readiness are removed from the Service load balancing / endpoints

incidents.question: Pods of our new reporting deployment stay Pending with the event 'Insufficient memory', although the two application containers request only 256Mi each and our nodes have about 4Gi of allocatable memory. The pod spec also has an init container that downloads and unpacks a large dataset and requests 6Gi of memory for the few seconds it runs. Why can't the scheduler place the pod, and how should we change the spec?
incidents.reference_answer: Init containers also affect the way Pod resource requirements are calculated for scheduling, autoscaling and quota management. Because init containers run in sequence before the application containers, which then run in parallel, the effective Pod-level request and limit values are the higher of two values: the highest request/limit of any init container, and the sum of the requests/limits of all application containers. Here the effective memory request is therefore max(6Gi, 2 x 256Mi) = 6Gi (calculation derived from the documented rule). The scheduler places Pods according to their requests (not their limits) and only considers nodes that still have enough capacity for the requested amounts. No node has 6Gi of allocatable memory, so the Pod stays Pending with 'Insufficient memory', although the running application would only need 512Mi. Kubernetes Patterns notes that this setup is not resource-efficient: even if the init container runs for a short time, the capacity it reserves cannot be used by other Pods. Fix: lower the memory request of the init container to what it really needs. Moving the heavy preparation out of the Pod (for example to a separate Job or to the image build) or using nodes with more allocatable memory are other options; these last suggestions are team recommendations, not stated in the source.
expected_answer_criteria: explains that the effective Pod-level request is the higher of the highest init container request and the sum of the application container requests
concludes that the effective memory request is 6Gi, more than the allocatable memory of any node
states that the scheduler places Pods according to their requests (not limits or actual usage)
proposes to reduce the init container request (or move the heavy initialization elsewhere) rather than the application requests

expected_investigation_steps: kubectl describe pod to read the FailedScheduling event

incidents.question: When one of our nodes ran short of memory last night, the kubelet evicted several batch pods, while the payment pods on the same node survived. None of the batch containers declare resources; the payment pods set memory and CPU requests equal to their limits. Is this behaviour expected, and how should we configure the batch pods if we want them to be less exposed?
incidents.reference_answer: Yes. The requests and limits declared (or omitted) for the containers define the Quality of Service (QoS) class of the Pod, which sets the order in which Pods are killed or evicted under resource pressure. A Pod without any requests and limits is Best-Effort: it has the lowest priority and is most likely killed first when the node runs out of incompressible resources such as memory. A Pod with requests lower than its limits is Burstable and is killed next if no Best-Effort Pods remain. A Pod whose requests equal its limits is Guaranteed: it has the highest priority and is not killed before Best-Effort and Burstable Pods. The batch pods were Best-Effort and the payment pods Guaranteed, so the order observed is the documented one: Kubernetes evicts BestEffort Pods first, then Burstable, and finally Guaranteed. To make the batch pods less exposed, declare memory and CPU requests and limits (Burstable), or requests equal to limits (Guaranteed) for the most critical ones, and check the resulting QoS class in kubectl describe pod.

recommends declaring requests and limits for the batch pods (Burstable or Guaranteed)

incidents.question: We added an init container that waits until the database migration service is available. Since then, new pods stay at STATUS Init:0/1 for twenty minutes and the main application container never starts, so its logs are empty. How do init containers explain this, and what should we check?
incidents.reference_answer: Init containers run before the application containers: they are executed in sequence, one by one, and all of them must terminate successfully before the application containers are started. An init container used to delay the start of a Pod while waiting for a dependency may not terminate until that dependency is satisfied. Here the init container keeps waiting for the migration service, so the Pod stays in its initialization phase and the application container is never started, which is why it has no logs. If an init container fails, the whole Pod is restarted (unless it is marked with RestartNever) and all init containers run again, so they should be idempotent. There is no readiness check for init containers. Check the logs and status of the init container itself (not the application container), and verify that the dependency it waits for (the migration service, its address and network access) is really available.

incidents.question: During every rolling update of our order service, a few in-flight requests fail and some temporary files are left behind on the volume. The old pods are killed about 30 seconds after the update starts, and our Node.js process does not handle any signal. What is Kubernetes doing when it stops these containers, and what should we change?
incidents.reference_answer: Whenever Kubernetes shuts down a container (because its Pod is shutting down, as in a rolling update, or because a failed liveness probe causes a restart), the container first receives a SIGTERM signal. SIGTERM is a gentle request to shut down cleanly: the application should finish its in-flight requests, release open connections and clean up temporary files, as quickly as possible. If the process has not stopped, Kubernetes sends SIGKILL after a grace period of 30 seconds by default; the grace period can be set per Pod with .spec.terminationGracePeriodSeconds. Since the Node.js process ignores SIGTERM, it keeps running until it is killed abruptly by SIGKILL after 30 seconds, losing in-flight requests and leaving temporary files. Fix: handle SIGTERM in the application to stop accepting work, finish in-flight requests and clean up, keep shutdown short, and raise terminationGracePeriodSeconds only if a clean shutdown really needs more than 30 seconds.

expected_investigation_steps: check whether the application handles SIGTERM

incidents.question: From pods scheduled on node worker-3, requests to the ClusterIP of every Service time out, while the same Services answer normally from pods on the other nodes. Pod-to-pod traffic using pod IPs still works from worker-3. Which component should we suspect, and why?
incidents.reference_answer: Suspect kube-proxy on worker-3. Cluster IPs are stable virtual IPs that load-balance traffic across the endpoints of a Service, and this is implemented by kube-proxy, a component that runs on every node. kube-proxy watches the Services through the API server and programs iptables rules in the kernel of its host to rewrite the destination of packets sent to a cluster IP towards one of the Service endpoints. If kube-proxy is not running or not working on one node, the iptables rules of that node are missing or stale: traffic to the virtual IPs fails from that node only, while direct pod-to-pod traffic, which does not depend on these rules, keeps working. Check that the kube-proxy pod (often run by a DaemonSet in kube-system) is running on worker-3, read its logs, inspect the node's iptables rules, and restart kube-proxy if needed.

incidents.question: On our bare-metal Kubernetes cluster, which has no cloud provider integration, we changed a Service to type LoadBalancer. Two hours later kubectl get services still shows EXTERNAL-IP <pending>. Why, and how can external clients reach the service in the meantime?
incidents.reference_answer: The LoadBalancer type relies on the cloud: it can be used if you have support from the cloud you are running on and your cluster is configured to take advantage of it. It builds on the NodePort type by additionally configuring the cloud to create a new load balancer directed at the cluster nodes. EXTERNAL-IP shows <pending> until the cloud has assigned an address; on a bare-metal cluster without cloud integration, nothing creates that load balancer, so the field stays pending. Because a LoadBalancer Service builds on NodePort, the system has picked a node port: every node of the cluster forwards traffic on that port to the Service. External clients can therefore reach the Service on any node's IP address at that node port (visible with kubectl describe service), or through an external load balancer configured to point at the nodes on that port.

incidents.question: We applied a NetworkPolicy that should block all ingress to the pods of our payments namespace except traffic coming from the api namespace. kubectl get networkpolicy -n payments shows the policy, yet a test pod in an unrelated namespace can still connect to the payments pods. What could explain that the policy has no effect?
incidents.reference_answer: A NetworkPolicy object is only enforced if the cluster network supports it: to create network policies, a container network interface (CNI) plugin that supports the NetworkPolicy API is required, and Kubernetes distributions support network policies to different degrees. If the CNI plugin does not implement network policies, the object is accepted by the API server but nothing filters the traffic, which matches the symptom. Also check the selection: Pods are selected with podSelector and/or namespaceSelector, and only a Pod selected by a policy becomes isolated and rejects the connections not explicitly allowed; by default no policy applies and traffic is unrestricted. A selector that does not match the payments pods leaves them unrestricted. Policy formatting may also differ depending on the CNI plugin. Verify which CNI plugin the cluster uses and whether it supports NetworkPolicy, check that the podSelector matches the pod labels, and consider a default policy that denies all ingress and egress, relaxed by explicit allow policies.

incidents.question: A penetration test reports that it could send requests to our Kubernetes API server without any token and still get answers on some endpoints, although RBAC is enabled. How is that possible, and what should we change on the API server?

incidents.question: A security review of our self-managed cluster found that the etcd members run on the same nodes as regular workloads and accept client connections from the whole node network. incidents.question: A teammate rebased our shared feature/payments branch onto main and force-pushed it. When I pulled, Git created a merge, and my history now contains duplicated commits with identical messages. What happened, and how can I bring my local work onto the rewritten branch cleanly?

For the team: avoid force-pushing shared branches; if history really must be rewritten on your own branch, prefer --force-with-lease, which fails if the remote ref is not the expected value and is safer than a plain force push.

incidents.question: Yesterday a teammate merged the unfinished feature branch billing-v2 into main and pushed it. Several colleagues have already pulled main and pushed new commits on top of that merge. We need the billing-v2 changes out of main today. Why is git reset not appropriate here, and how do we undo the merge?
incidents.reference_answer: Resetting main to the commit before the merge would rewrite history: if other people have the commits you are rewriting, you should avoid reset, and the approach does not work anyway when other commits have been created since the merge, because moving the branch pointer would lose those changes. For a merge commit, use git revert -m 1 <merge-commit>: the -m 1 flag indicates which parent is the mainline to keep. The first parent is main as it was before the merge, the second is the tip of billing-v2, so the revert undoes all the changes brought by billing-v2 while keeping the content of main. Then push the revert commit normally. When billing-v2 is ready, first un-revert the original merge (revert the revert commit) to bring back the reverted changes, then merge billing-v2 again.

incidents.question: We migrated a legacy daemon to a systemd unit with Type=forking, but the program actually stays in the foreground. systemctl start hangs for a long time, then the unit is marked failed with a timeout, even though the application was serving requests during that time. What is happening and how should the unit be corrected?
incidents.reference_answer: With Type=forking, systemd expects the ExecStart= process to fork and the parent process to exit when start-up is complete. A program that stays in the foreground never does that, so systemd keeps waiting for the start-up completion signal.
